name: Prepositions
moduleIntroduction:
Welcome to the module on Prepositions! Prepositions are small but very important words like in, on, at, to, and from. They show the relationship between things, telling us where something is, when something happens, or where it is going.

This is a big challenge for Francophone students because French often uses one word where English uses many. For example, the French word 'à' can mean at, on, or in depending on the situation ("à Yaoundé", "à 8h00"). You cannot just translate "à" to "at". English has different rules. For example, we say "in Yaoundé" but "at the market". This module will teach you the English patterns for time, place, and movement so you can choose the correct preposition with confidence.
contrastiveExplanation:
The main problem with prepositions is direct translation. French à, en, dans, and sur do not map perfectly to English at, in, and on. You must learn the English logic.

Prepositions of Time (IN / ON / AT):

IN is for long periods (like a container of time):
Examples: in 2024, in August, in the morning, in two weeks.
French: "en 2024", "au mois d'août", "dans la matinée".

ON is for specific days and dates (like a date on a calendar page):
Examples: on Monday, on my birthday, on October 1st.
French: "lundi" (no preposition), "le 1er octobre". This is a big difference! English needs 'on'.

AT is for specific times (like a point on a clock):
Examples: at 8:00 PM, at noon, at night.
French: "à 8h00", "à midi". This is similar, but 'at night' is different from "la nuit".

Tip: Think of a pyramid. IN is the big base (months, years). ON is in the middle (days, dates). AT is the small point (clock time).

Prepositions of Place (IN / ON / AT):

IN is for inside a container or a large area:
Examples: in the classroom, in Cameroon, in Yaoundé.
French: "dans la classe", "au Cameroun", "à Yaoundé". French uses 'à' for cities, but English always uses 'in'.

ON is for a surface:
Examples: on the table, on the floor, on the wall.
French: "sur la table". This is often similar.

AT is for a specific point or location:
Examples: at the bus stop, at school, at the market.
French: "à l'arrêt de bus", "à l'école", "au marché".

Prepositions of Movement (TO / FROM / INTO):

TO shows direction towards a destination.
Example: "I am going to Douala."
French: "Je vais à Douala." (Using 'à').

FROM shows the origin.
Example: "He is coming from the village."
French: "Il vient du village." (Using 'de').

The error comes when translating "at" for "to".
❌ "I am going at the market." (French "Je vais au marché" (à+le)).
✅ "I am going to the market."

commonErrors.frenchConnection: French uses "à" for cities ("à Yaoundé"). Students translate "à" directly to "at". English must use "in" for cities and countries.

commonErrors.wrong: The meeting is on Monday, at the morning.
commonErrors.correct: The meeting is on Monday, in the morning.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French "dans la matinée" or "le matin" is confusing. English always uses "in the morning", "in the afternoon", and "in the evening". (But "at night"!)

commonErrors.wrong: We have our exam in Friday.
commonErrors.correct: We have our exam on Friday.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French often uses no preposition for days ("Nous avons l'examen vendredi"). Students guess 'in'. English must use "on" for days of the week.

commonErrors.wrong: I will see you at 8:00 PM in the night.
commonErrors.correct: I will see you at 8:00 PM at night.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: "Dans la nuit" (in the night) is correct in French, but the English fixed expression is "at night".
French "Elle va à l'école". "À" (to) is confused with "at" (location). For movement/direction, English uses "to".

commonErrors.wrong: The students are in the school compound.
commonErrors.correct: The students are at the school compound.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French "dans" (in) is common. "At" is used for a general location or area. Use "in" only if you mean inside an enclosed space.
Another "à" (to) vs. "at" (location) error. Movement towards a place uses "to".

commonErrors.wrong: I was born in 1990, in October 5th.
commonErrors.correct: I was born in 1990, on October 5th.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: You use "in" for the year (in 1990), but "on" for a specific date (on October 5th).
This is a dependent preposition error. French "avoir peur de". "De" is translated to "from", but the correct English phrase is "afraid of".

commonErrors.wrong: He is married with a woman from Bafoussam.
commonErrors.correct: He is married to a woman from Bafoussam.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French "marié avec...". "Avec" is "with". The correct English phrase is "married to".

commonErrors.wrong: I must listen at the teacher.
commonErrors.correct: I must listen to the teacher.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French "écouter le professeur" (no preposition). Students add the wrong one. The English verb 'listen' must be followed by "to".
French "dépend de...". "De" is translated as "of". The correct English phrase is "depend on".

commonErrors.wrong: He arrived to the motor park.
commonErrors.correct: He arrived at the motor park.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: You "go to" a place, but you "arrive at" a specific location. French "Il est arrivé au (à+le) parc..." causes the confusion.

commonErrors.wrong: Different of my brother, I like music.
commonErrors.correct: Different from my brother, I like music.
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French "différent de". "De" is translated to "of". The correct English phrase is "different from" (or "different to" in British English).
French "participer à". Students may translate to "of". The correct English phrase is "participate in".

items.questionText: My birthday is ___ August.
items.feedback: Correct! We use IN for long periods of time, including months (in August), years (in 2025), and seasons (in the dry season).

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Mon anniversaire est en août."
(French uses "en" for months, which is a common equivalent for "in".)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"My birthday is in August."
(English uses "in" for long periods like months, seasons, and years.)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: This is not the hardest error, as "en" often maps to "in". The confusion arises when students mix this up with "on" (for days) and "at" (for times). The French "au mois d'août" (in the month of August) can also add confusion.

items.questionText: The school re-opens ___ September 15th.
items.feedback: Excellent! We use ON for specific days and dates. Because this is a full date (September 15th), we must use 'on'.

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"L'école rouvre le 15 septembre."
(French uses the definite article "le" (the) before a specific date.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"The school re-opens on September 15th."
(English *must* use the preposition "on" for all specific days and dates.)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French does not use a preposition like "on" in this case ("le 15"). Students translating this logic either use "the" (a direct translation of "le") or no preposition at all. They must learn the English rule: **Day/Date = ON**.

items.questionText: Our first class starts ___ 7:30 AM.
items.feedback: That's right! We use AT for specific clock times (at 7:30 AM, at noon, at midnight).

items.questionText: I always study ___ the evening after dinner.
items.feedback: Perfect! We use IN for parts of the day: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. (Exception: at night!)

items.questionText: Find the error: "Muna always brushes his teeth in the morning, but he forgets in night."
items.feedback: You found it! We say "IN the morning", "IN the afternoon", and "IN the evening", but the expression for night is different: "AT night".

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Il oublie la nuit" or "dans la nuit".
(French can use "la nuit" (the night) or "dans la nuit" (in the night) depending on the context.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"He forgets at night."
(English uses fixed expressions: "in the morning", "in the afternoon", "in the evening", but it *must* be "at night".)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: Students learn "in the morning/afternoon" and logically apply it, saying "in the night". This is a direct translation of "dans la nuit" and seems to follow the pattern, but "at night" is a fixed, idiomatic exception.

items.questionText: I live ___ a small neighborhood ___ Yaoundé.
items.feedback: Perfect! We use IN for cities (in Yaoundé) and also for enclosed areas like a neighborhood (in a neighborhood). French uses "à Yaoundé", which is why this is tricky.

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"J'habite dans un petit quartier à Yaoundé."
(French uses "dans" (in) for an enclosed area, but "à" for a city.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"I live in a small neighborhood in Yaoundé."
(English uses "in" for both the enclosed area (neighborhood) and the large area (city, country).)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: This is a major, high-frequency error. French *always* uses "à" before a city name ("à Yaoundé", "à Douala"). Students translate "à" directly to "at". They *must* learn the English rule: **Cities & Countries = IN**.

items.questionText: Please wait for me ___ the motor park entrance.
items.feedback: Correct! We use AT to talk about a specific point or location (at the entrance, at the bus stop, at the market).

items.questionText: Don't write ___ the wall of the classroom!
items.feedback: That's right. A wall is a surface. We write or put things ON a surface (on the wall, on the table, on the floor).

items.questionText: Find the error: "The teacher is standing in the front of the class."
items.feedback: Good catch! The correct expression is "at the front of" (meaning "à l'avant de"). "In the front of" is not correct in this context.

items.questionText: We are travelling ___ Bamenda tomorrow.
items.feedback: Yes! When we talk about movement towards a destination, we use TO. French "aller à..." often causes students to use 'at' by mistake.

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Nous voyageons à Bamenda demain."
(French uses "à" to show direction/destination.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"We are travelling to Bamenda tomorrow."
(English *must* use "to" to show movement or direction towards a destination.)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: This is the *other* "à" problem. Students confuse the French "à" (destination) with the English "at" (location). They mean "to" but say "at". (e.g., "I go *at* school" instead of "I go *to* school").

items.questionText: The bus is coming ___ Bafoussam.
items.feedback: Correct! We use FROM to show the origin or starting point (like French "de" or "du").

items.questionText: My father arrived ___ the village late last night.
items.feedback: Excellent! This is tricky. We say "go TO" a place, but "arrive AT" a place. This is a fixed English pattern you must memorize.

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Mon père est arrivé au village (à + le) tard hier soir."
(French uses "à" (in its 'au' form) for "arriver".)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"My father arrived at the village..."
(English uses "arrive at" for a specific point/location and "arrive in" for a large area (city/country). We do *not* use "arrive to".)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: Because "go to", "travel to", and "come to" are correct, students assume "arrive to" is also correct. This is reinforced by the French "arriver à". They must learn that "arrive" is a special verb that takes "at" or "in".

items.questionText: Please listen ___ your parents. They have good advice.
items.feedback: That's right! The verb 'listen' must be followed by the preposition 'to'. We say "listen to someone". French says "écouter quelqu'un" (no preposition), which causes this error.

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Tu dois écouter tes parents."
(The French verb "écouter" (to listen to) is a transitive verb and does not require a preposition. It directly takes an object.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"You must listen to your parents."
(The English verb "listen" is intransitive in this context and *must* be followed by the preposition "to" before its object.)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: This is a "verb + preposition" (phrasal verb) error. Students translate "écouter" directly to "listen" and omit the "to" because it's not needed in French.

items.questionText: Njoya is married ___ a teacher from Douala.
items.feedback: Correct! This is a common error. French says "marié avec" ("with"), but the correct English phrase is "married TO".

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Mon frère est marié avec une enseignante."
(French uses the preposition "avec" (with) for this expression.)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"My brother is married to a teacher."
(English *must* use the fixed expression "be married to".)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: This is a direct translation error of a fixed expression. "Avec" = "with", so students say "married with". This is a very common and noticeable mistake.

visualHighlighting.incorrect: My brother is married *with* a teacher.
visualHighlighting.correct: My brother is married *to* a teacher.

items.questionText: Find the error: "This lesson depends of the teacher."
items.feedback: You found it! French says "dépend de" ("of"), but the correct English verb phrase is "to depend ON".

frenchComparison.frenchStructure:
"Cette leçon dépend du (de + le) professeur."
(French uses the preposition "de" (of/from) in the expression "dépendre de".)
frenchComparison.englishStructure:
"This lesson depends on the teacher."
(English *must* use the fixed expression "to depend on".)
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: Another direct translation of a fixed "verb + preposition" phrase. "De" = "of", so students say "depends of".

items.questionText: The rainy season in Limbe starts ___ March.
items.feedback: Correct! We use IN for long periods of time, including months (in March), years, and seasons.

items.questionText: The national holiday is ___ May 20th.
items.feedback: Excellent! We use ON for specific days and dates. Because this is a full date (May 20th), we must use 'on'.

items.questionText: The school assembly begins ___ 7:00 AM sharp.
items.feedback: That's right! We use AT for specific clock times (at 7:00 AM, at noon, at midnight).

items.questionText: I do my homework ___ the afternoon before dinner.
items.feedback: Perfect! We use IN for parts of the day: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening.

items.questionText: Find the error: "I will call you on the afternoon."
items.feedback: You found it! We use IN for parts of the day: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. We don't use "on" for these expressions.

items.questionText: My aunt works ___ an office ___ Douala.
items.feedback: Perfect! We use IN for enclosed spaces (in an office) and also for cities (in Douala).

items.questionText: I will meet you ___ the carrefour (crossroads).
items.feedback: Correct! We use AT to talk about a specific point or location (at the carrefour, at the corner, at the junction).

items.questionText: Put the chalk ___ the teacher's desk, not on the floor.
items.feedback: That's right! A desk is a surface. We put things ON a surface (on the desk, on the table, on the floor).

items.questionText: Find the error: "There is a map in the back of the book."
items.feedback: Good catch! The correct expression is "at the back of" (meaning "à l'arrière de"). "In the back of" is not correct in this context.

items.questionText: Ekane is going ___ the market to buy plantains.
items.feedback: Yes! When we talk about movement towards a destination, we use TO. French "aller à..." often causes students to use 'at' by mistake.

items.questionText: My cousin is coming ___ Kribi for the holidays.
items.feedback: Correct! We use FROM to show the origin or starting point (like French "de" or "du").

items.questionText: What time did you arrive ___ home yesterday?
items.feedback: Excellent! This is very tricky. We say "arrive AT the village" or "arrive AT school", but with 'home', we use NO preposition. We just say "arrive home".

items.questionText: Please look ___ me when I am speaking.
items.feedback: That's right! The verb 'look' is followed by 'at' when you mean to direct your eyes toward someone. We say "look at someone".

items.questionText: Foncha is not related ___ the headmaster.
items.feedback: Correct! The correct English phrase is "related TO". French uses "lié à" or "apparenté à", so the preposition 'to' is similar.

items.questionText: Find the error: "Your success depends of your hard work."
items.feedback: You found it! French says "dépend de" ("of"), but the correct English verb phrase is "to depend ON".
